scope: Conservative one-sided in-period floor for the Great Zimbabwe settlement, with explicit archaeological disagreement and urban-boundary containment.

promotion_audit.decision: Promote only the conservative 10,000-person floor stated by the UNESCO World Heritage record for the fourteenth-century city. Do not use the older 18,000-20,000 estimate, the PLOS <10,000 revised estimate, or the urban population as a two-sided carrying-capacity interval. The lower bound is a containment constraint on the EU5 location that contains the archaeological site; it is not a regional or continental target.

records.label: Great Zimbabwe fourteenth-century archaeological urban population floor
records.interval_semantics: This is a one-sided locally supported population floor, not a complete population interval or capacity ceiling. UNESCO's World Heritage record says that Great Zimbabwe was the principal city of a major state in the fourteenth century and that its population exceeded 10,000. The floor is kept at 10,000 exactly because Chirikure et al. (2017) find that the commonly repeated 18,000-20,000 figure is not supported and conclude that the total site population was unlikely to have exceeded 10,000. The disagreement is retained rather than converted into artificial uncertainty.
pressure_evidence: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Outstanding Universal Value, paragraphs 52-61: the property was built and occupied from approximately 1100 to 1450; in the fourteenth century it was the principal city of a major state, its population exceeded 10,000, and the hinterland could no longer furnish food for the overpopulated city when the capital was abandoned around 1450.

UNESCO, paragraphs 59-61: farming and pastoral activities are documented by the archaeological record, while imported glass, porcelain, beads and coins show long-distance prestige/trade connections. Staple local production is therefore plausible but not treated as autarky.

Chirikure et al. (2017), PLOS ONE 12(6):e0178335, abstract and pp. 1-2: archaeological chronology, phosphate/geophysical settlement evidence, demographic back-projection and ecological consistency checks reject the unqualified 20,000-person assumption and place the credible total below 10,000. Their analysis explicitly evaluates agricultural land, cattle pasture, water and environmental sustainability.

Chirikure et al. (2017), pp. 9-11: a 20,000-person scenario would require approximately 20,000 hectares of arable land and 11,500-20,000 cattle, while local stocking rates and the absence of the expected environmental degradation make that scenario ecologically implausible. This is independent pressure/resource evidence, not a regional multiplier.
records.trade_dependence: mixed: staple calories were supplied by nearby farming and pastoral systems, while Great Zimbabwe was an exchange hub connected to Indian Ocean trade and tribute networks; imported prestige goods are not counted as food imports.
records.boundary_description: The UNESCO Great Zimbabwe National Monument property and its associated settlement, approximately 800 ha, at about 30 km from modern Masvingo. This is the archaeological city/site boundary, not the full Zimbabwe state, Victoria District, or a modern administrative province.
records.boundary_source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Outstanding Universal Value, paragraphs 52-69; Chirikure et al. (2017), Fig. 1-2 and pp. 1-2.
records.source_family_independence: UNESCO's World Heritage synthesis and the open-access PLOS archaeological/ecological study are independent institutional assessments of the site, but both concern the same archaeological settlement and are treated as one source family. No starting-population or HYDE field is used.
citation_details: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Outstanding Universal Value, paragraphs 52-61: date, >10,000 population statement, farming/pastoral evidence, trade evidence and food-hinterland failure.

Chirikure, Moultrie, Bandama, Dandara and Manyanga (2017), PLOS ONE 12(6):e0178335, abstract, pp. 1-2 and 9-11: archaeological population controversy, <10,000 revised conclusion, chronology, land/pasture/water checks and sustainability interpretation.
records.notes: The floor is deliberately conservative at the intersection of UNESCO's >10,000 statement and Chirikure et al.'s revised <10,000 conclusion. It is useful as a one-sided test of whether the containing EU5 location can support a locally provisioned medieval urban site. It must not be treated as a two-sided Malthusian capacity interval, and no Great Zimbabwe, Zimbabwe, or Africa-specific correction is permitted.
